items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: on the floor sitting at his feet was Charlie Shavers, the great trumpet player and a terrific — what a great guy Charlie was.

ctx.x: Okay. Well I’m going to — in the time I have then I’m going to leapfrog ahead, but only a little bit. Because I wanted to ask you about young Dan goes to Harlem. And I had heard a radio interview that you did, about going up to Harlem and checking out the music and stuff. I wonder what — can you describe like what a night would be like?

Well this was not too terribly long after I came to New York and I had met this little underground trumpet player named Matt Lorber, nickname was “Face”; he knew everybody and everybody knew him, and also met a very hip young lady who was the first to take me to the Apollo Theater in Harlem, and that actually turned out to be a night when Dizzy’s big band was appearing there with Chano Pozo, so I got to see that, which was tremendous. The Apollo was — one thing of course — the Apollo was frequented to some extent…

going, but it wasn’t what it used to be. But there were little clubs and there was this wonderful trumpet player and singer named Hot Lips Page. Lips was my friend, Nat was a kind of protégé of Lips’. Lips was from Texas and he didn’t call him “Face” but he called him “Shorty” which was pronounced “Shouty” — that was his Texas accent. And going to Harlem, Lips lived there, was a wonderful experience. There were after hours places, and the after hours places could be somebody’s apartment where there was an old…

items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Charlie Shavers had a great little group there. That was when [Hot] Lips [Page] sat in with Charlie... Very often Charlie Shavers was there for quite a while. I remember one night when Dinah Shore came in... Roy was the first guy that I ever encountered who played flugelhorn... and Charlie was on tr

ctx.x: Yeah. He became a Billy Graham accolade. But that was another side. Lonnie was a pretty good piano player. He would occasionally – very rarely he might sit in on a jam session. He had been to New England Conservatory. He was a talented composer. Lonnie’s still around. He’s older than me. He’s now in his 80s. Except for a brief period, when he was associated with Charlie Mingus and made an album on Mingus’s Debut label which has never been reissued, but one track was reissued in this big Debut CD package which…

Floyd Campbell on washboard, Buster Bailey on clarinet, and James P. Johnson on piano. That was an incredible thing to see in the late 1940s, early 1950s. It was already a chunk of bygone history. All sorts of people that he would have. He seemed to know everybody. Then a few years later, after I got back out of the Army – we’ll come to that later – when I was hanging out at the Copper Rail in mid-Manhattan, one day suddenly Bob Maltz came in and said, “Has anybody seen Art Blakey?” That seemed like such a…

items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He would play in a little club up there. It wasn't Albany, but somewhere near there. On a weekend, he would get people like Roy Eldridge, Charlie Shaver, and Teddy Wilson to come up and sit in with him. Somebody recorded some of that.

ctx.x: As a writer. There were people in California. First of all, his good friend whom he had traveled with was somebody who had – he had a porcelain factory in Austria which was taken over by his Christian partner, but they managed to tweak out money to him. Also my father had one good friend, a movie director named John Brahm, who is best known for a film noir called The Lodger, which is a Jack-the-Ripper film, which starred a good but unfortunate actor named Laird Cregar. I don't know if you knew him. Laird Cregar…

Then they had – of course it was important to arrange some kind of schooling for me. I enjoyed it, not having to go to school. I could see American movies for the first time in a long time. There was a boarding school outside of Stockholm where I then was sent along with a bunch of Danish kids my age and some Norwegians as well. Fairly recently – you know that we're on this jazz research list on the internet. There's one Norwegian there who is part of it, Arne Neegaard. We figured – he's the one who first figured…
